strengths: Soundness: Equation 5 gives a simple, implementable modification that lets image tokens attend to the question while keeping answer generation causal. Restricting the unlocked attention to the input avoids the obvious target-leakage problem for single-turn supervised training, without adding parameters.

Empirical merit: Table 1 compares MMA with causal attention and CCA using the same backbone, datasets, and training schedule. The reported improvements span general, knowledge, and vision-centric tasks; examples over CCA include LLaVA-Bench increasing from 54.0 to 59.6 and CV-Bench2D from 56.0 to 57.8. These controlled comparisons provide useful evidence beyond comparisons with independently trained models.

Presentation and reproducibility: The attention-mask diagrams and equations make the central intervention understandable. The appendices provide optimizer settings, dataset sampling probabilities, training and evaluation prompts, hardware, decoding settings, and benchmark breakdowns.

Significance and limitations: A lightweight way to improve question-conditioned visual representations could be practically useful. The paper appropriately acknowledges caption-pretraining leakage and explicitly discloses using only the first image for interleaved MMMU examples.
weaknesses: Originality is insufficiently established. Bidirectional attention over multimodal input prefixes with causal answer decoding is an established design, including in models such as PaliGemma. The related-work discussion focuses on connectors, data, and CCA without positioning MMA against this closely related approach. MMA preserves causal within-modality attention at each layer, but the paper neither establishes why that distinction matters nor compares against a fully bidirectional input-prefix mask. The repeated characterization of this direction as fundamentally unexplored is therefore unconvincing.

Soundness: Important numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in the headline gains. Table 1 reports MMA MME perception as 1363.7, whereas Table 7 reports 1344.9; MMA MMB is 71.8 in Table 1 but 70.3 in Table 8. The stated 4.3% MMB improvement agrees with 70.3, not 71.8. These discrepancies need reconciliation, followed by a transparent recomputation of the advertised 7.2% average, including the RealWorldQA regression.

Evaluation comparability needs clarification. In Table 11, all per-subject MMMU scores for the baseline, DOT, MMA, and AKI occur in increments of 20 percentage points, whereas CCA scores have much finer increments. This suggests potentially different evaluation sample counts or splits, although the manuscript does not establish the cause. Exact splits and denominators are essential before treating these results as matched comparisons. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates are supplied, leaving smaller improvements, such as POPE 81.9 to 82.7, difficult to assess.

The experiments do not sufficiently isolate or generalize the proposed mechanism. They use one LLM, vision encoder, connector, and visual-token configuration. Missing controls include a fully bidirectional input prefix and bidirectional image-only attention. DOT also receives additional training, so its occasional improvements do not isolate cross-modal visibility from extra optimization. The final extended-training AKI model has no matched causal-attention counterpart, preventing attribution of its gains to MMA rather than additional training and OCR data.

Significance is overstated relative to the results. Table 2 establishes competitiveness on selected tasks, rather than superiority over similarly sized models on most benchmarks: BLIP-3-4B exceeds AKI on most listed metrics. Other modalities and interleaved inputs are not experimentally evaluated. Equation 6 is a plausible extension, but does not establish the claimed generic scalability. Likewise, broad benchmark improvements and selected examples provide limited evidence for the stronger mechanistic claim that MMA resolves vision-language misalignment.

The claim of no additional training cost is not adequately supported. Appendix A supplies coarse training durations, but no matched throughput, memory, or inference-prefill measurements. Allowing additional attention edges and using a nonstandard mask can affect computation and optimized-kernel compatibility even without adding parameters. Reproduction also requires clarification of the final data budget: 250,000 KALE steps at batch size 192 imply 48 million sample presentations, while Appendix B describes approximately 100 million sampled KALE pairs.

The broader-impact discussion describes benefits almost exclusively, without substantively discussing residual hallucination risks, biases, or privacy and licensing considerations for the web-derived data. Appendix A also states that no deduplication is performed, but provides no assessment of training–benchmark overlap. These are reporting and evaluation limitations, not evidence of misconduct; the decisive reasons for rejection remain the unresolved novelty, comparability, and result-consistency issues.

strengths: Soundness: The single-image method is simple and technically plausible. Equation 5 lets image tokens attend to the question while excluding answer tokens, preserving autoregressive answer generation without adding parameters.

Significance: Table 1 provides useful controlled evidence under a shared backbone, dataset, and training schedule. MMA improves substantially over conventional causal attention, including MMB (64.9 to 71.8) and CV-Bench2D (45.2 to 57.8), and generally outperforms CCA.

Presentation and reproducibility: The mask definition and diagrams make the implementation understandable. The appendices provide model identifiers, hyperparameters, dataset sampling probabilities, prompt templates, hardware, and evaluation details.

Limitations: Section 6.2 appropriately identifies indirect information leakage when applying the mask to caption pretraining. Restricting the demonstrated method to question-conditioned SFT is a reasonable design choice.
weaknesses: Originality: The claimed fundamentally unexplored architectural direction is insufficiently established relative to prefix-LM and bidirectional input attention. There is neither substantive positioning against these designs nor a fully bidirectional image-question prefix baseline. Consequently, the paper does not establish why its particular modality-dependent mask is necessary or what new understanding it provides beyond relaxing prefix causality.

Soundness and reporting: Central results disagree across tables. MMA's MME perception score is 1363.7 in Table 1 but 1344.9 in Table 7; MMB is 71.8 in Table 1 but 70.3 in Table 8. Table 1 reports gains of 10.9% and 4.3%, whereas its displayed scores imply approximately 12.5% and 6.5%. Averaging the relative improvements across all 12 displayed columns gives approximately 6.85%, rather than the headline 7.2%. These discrepancies need reconciliation before the aggregate claim can be trusted.

Soundness: The experiments do not adequately isolate the proposed explanation. DOT doubles training exposure and changes the training curriculum, without an equally long conventional-training control or a fixed-budget mixed-order baseline. Its gains therefore do not establish the importance of mutual attention. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of smaller MMA-versus-CCA improvements, such as POPE's 0.8-point gain.

Efficiency: No additional parameters does not establish unchanged training cost. A noncausal mask can affect attention-kernel efficiency, memory, and prefill time. Appendix A provides approximate training durations, but no sufficiently detailed matched timing or memory comparison supports the repeated claim of no additional training cost. DOT's factorial cost also follows from enumerating every permutation, rather than being an inherent requirement of order augmentation.

Significance and scope: All controlled experiments use one backbone and one single-image configuration. The extended-training AKI model has no matched causal-attention control, so its results cannot isolate MMA from additional training and OCR data. Table 2 shows competitiveness rather than broad superiority: AKI leads the smaller-model group on only MME perception and LLaVA-Bench, while lagging several alternatives elsewhere. Claims about other modalities and interleaved inputs remain untested.

Reproducibility and research ethics: Dataset exposure requires clarification: Appendix B reports approximately 100 million sampled KALE pairs for AKI, while 250,000 steps at global batch size 192 provide 48 million sample presentations. Exact evaluation splits and sampling procedures also need clearer documentation. The explicit absence of deduplication warrants a train–evaluation overlap analysis, without implying contamination has occurred. The broader-impact section discusses prospective benefits but gives little attention to residual hallucination, bias, or privacy risks.

strengths: Significance: Question-conditioned visual representations address a useful problem. MMA is a simple attention-mask modification that adds no parameters and can be incorporated into an existing decoder-based MLLM.

Soundness: Table 1 provides controlled comparisons with causal attention and CCA using the same backbone and datasets. Reported improvements span general, knowledge, and vision-centric evaluations; for example, CV-Bench2D increases from 56.0 with CCA to 57.8 with MMA.

Presentation and reproducibility: The core mask is explicitly defined in Equation 5. The appendices provide training hyperparameters, hardware, dataset sampling probabilities, prompt templates, decoding settings, and category-level results.

Limitations: The paper appropriately acknowledges caption-pretraining leakage and restricts MMA to the conditioning input during supervised finetuning. This is a sensible boundary, and the disclosure itself is a strength.
weaknesses: Soundness: Central results are internally inconsistent. MMA's MME perception score is 1363.7 in Table 1 but 1344.9 in Table 7; its MMBench score is 71.8 in Table 1 but 70.3 in Table 8. The corresponding improvement percentages match the appendix values rather than Table 1. The headline 7.2% also matches the average of the 11 positive entries, excluding the RealWorldQA regression, rather than an average across all 12 evaluations. These discrepancies require reconciliation before the reported aggregate gain can be trusted.

Originality: The paper does not adequately distinguish MMA from established prefix-LM and bidirectional conditioning attention. Its distinctive choice is to unlock cross-modal attention while retaining causal within-modality masks, but there is no comparison against a fully bidirectional image-question prefix. Without this baseline and appropriate positioning, the claimed fundamentally unexplored architectural contribution is insufficiently established.

Evaluation reliability: The MMMU split and sample counts are unspecified. In Table 11, every subject score for the proposed models and causal baseline is a multiple of 20%, whereas CCA has much finer increments. This unexplained pattern raises a concrete question about whether identical evaluation subsets were used. No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates establish the reliability of smaller gains, such as POPE's 0.8-point improvement over CCA.

Efficiency: Unchanged parameter count and training steps do not establish unchanged training time. The paper provides approximate training durations but no matched throughput, memory, or latency measurements, nor sufficient attention-kernel implementation details to substantiate the repeated claim of no additional training cost.

Significance and scope: Experiments use one language backbone, one vision encoder, and single-image inputs. The extended-training AKI model lacks a correspondingly trained causal-attention control, so its improvements cannot be separated from longer training and added OCR data. Table 2 shows outright best performance on only two of the 12 columns, which does not support the introduction's claim of superiority over similarly sized models across most benchmarks.

Reproducibility and ethics: Detailed recipes are helpful, but exact evaluation subsets and sampled pretraining data remain unclear, and Appendix A explicitly reports no deduplication without a benchmark-overlap analysis. The broader-impact section discusses applications almost exclusively, leaving dataset provenance, privacy, and risks from residual hallucinations largely unaddressed. These are reporting gaps rather than evidence of misconduct.
